blocks.text: A chat template is a set of rules that turns a structured list of role tagged messages, system, user, assistant, into the single flat text string a model actually reads, inserting the special tokens that mark where each turn and role begins and ends.

Getting this exactly right matters more than it might seem, since a mismatched or incorrectly applied template is one of the most common silent bugs in fine-tuning, degrading quality without throwing any visible error.
1. What a Chat Template Does
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359753-894433790.png

Internally, a model does not see a structured list of role tagged messages, it sees one continuous sequence of tokens. A chat template defines exactly how to flatten a conversation into that sequence, inserting markers that tell the model where the system prompt ends, where the user turn is, and where the assistant is expected to respond.
2. Special Tokens That Mark Roles and Turns

blocks.alt: Special Tokens That Mark Roles and Turns
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359754-376402240.png

Chat templates rely on special tokens, reserved sequences that do not appear in normal text, to mark role boundaries, where the system message ends and the user turn begins, and where one assistant response ends and the next user turn starts.
These special tokens are what let the model reliably distinguish structure from content, even though everything is ultimately just one flat sequence of tokens.
3. Why Templates Differ Across Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359754-42389578.png

Different model families define their own chat template conventions, different special tokens, different ordering, different ways of marking the system prompt, chosen by whichever team trained that particular model.

This means a template that works correctly for one model will almost certainly produce garbled or incorrectly structured input if applied to a different model family, since the special tokens themselves may not even exist in the other model vocabulary.

blocks.text: 4. Applying a Chat Template Before Tokenization

blocks.alt: Applying a Chat Template Before Tokenization
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359754-55549072.png

The typical pipeline order is, structure the conversation as a list of role tagged messages, apply the chat template to flatten it into one text string, then tokenize that flattened string, exactly as covered in more depth in the upcoming Tokenization Pipeline topic.

code.content:
# A simplified chat template application, conceptually
formatted_text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"},
    ],
    tokenize=False
)
token_ids = tokenizer(formatted_text)

blocks.text: 5. Training and Inference Must Use the Same Template

blocks.alt: Training and Inference Must Use the Same Template
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359755-802067135.png

A fine-tuned model learns to expect input structured exactly the way its training data was templated. If a different template, or no template at all, is applied at inference time, the model receives input that looks structurally unfamiliar, and quality can drop noticeably even though nothing about the underlying request actually changed.

blocks.title: The single most common silent fine-tuning bug
blocks.content: A quiet mismatch between the training time template and the inference time template is one of the most frequent, hardest to notice sources of unexpectedly poor fine-tuned model output.

blocks.text: 6. System Prompts Inside a Template
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359755-622649832.png

Most chat templates define a specific place and format for the system prompt, the overarching instructions that apply across the whole conversation, distinct from the individual user and assistant turns.
Where and how the system prompt is wrapped varies by model family, which is another reason templates cannot simply be copied between different base models without verification.
7. Verifying a Template Is Applied Correctly

Before launching a full training run, it is worth printing out a few fully templated examples and inspecting them by eye, confirming the special tokens appear where expected and the overall structure matches what the target model documentation describes.
8. Mismatched Templates, A Common Silent Bug

blocks.alt: Mismatched Templates, A Common Silent Bug
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359755-342704656.png

Because a mismatched template does not usually cause an outright error, the model still produces some output, it is easy for this bug to go undetected until someone notices the fine-tuned model behaves worse than expected, without an obvious cause.
9. Chat Templates and Fine-Tuning Consistency

Every conversation dataset covered in the previous topic of this module ultimately needs to pass through a chat template before training, making this a required, not optional, step in the dataset preparation pipeline whenever the fine-tuning target is a chat style model.
Worked Example

A team fine-tunes a model using a conversation dataset, applying what they believe is the correct chat template. After training, the model performs noticeably worse than expected on straightforward questions.

Investigating, they discover their formatting script was using a generic template rather than the specific one documented for their chosen base model, meaning the special tokens the model actually expects never appeared correctly in training. Reformatting the dataset with the correct model specific template and retraining resolves the quality gap entirely.
Common Mistakes

items: Copying a chat template from a different model family without verifying it matches the target model
Using a different template at inference time than the one used during training
Never manually inspecting a fully templated example before starting a training run
Assuming poor fine-tuned model quality is a data or hyperparameter problem without first checking the template

blocks.text: Practice

Find the documented chat template for a specific model you are interested in, and manually trace through how a simple two turn conversation would be flattened into text under that template, noting exactly where each special token appears.
Key Takeaway

A chat template flattens structured, role tagged conversation data into the exact text format a specific model expects, and since this format differs across model families and must match precisely between training and inference, verifying the correct template is applied is one of the simplest checks that prevents one of the most common silent fine-tuning bugs.
